::: {.letter-metadata}
**Date:** December 8, 1896.  
**From:** Elderfield, Otterbourne, Winchester  
**Manuscript:** MS location unknown.  Printed in Coleridge, [<i>Life</i>](other_books/otherbook_40.qmd), 338
:::

Dear [M. E. C.](people/person_294.qmd)
I feel strongly impelled to write to you both to thank you for your letter and for St. Christopher's legend.  A German lady once sent me a set of photographs of frescoes of his history, where he was going through all sorts of temptations, including one by evil women.

I think I must tell you that the [*Daisy Chain*](cmy_books/cmybook_24.qmd) was written just when I was fresh from the influence and guiding of [my father](people/person_1631.qmd).  Not that he was in the least like Dr. May, being a soldier with the highest chivalrous sense of nobleness and justice, and moreover with a strong desire to see, and do everything in the best way possible.

I remember his exclaiming, when Norman's health began to fail, ‘You don't mean to kill him?’ and that seems to me to mark how far I had gone on in that story.  The [*Heir of Redclyffe*](cmy_books/cmybook_15.qmd) he had looked over and criticised with all his might.

Another advantage the *Daisy Chain*  had was, that coming out in monthly parts there was a good deal of friendly, often merry discussion of the characters, with such friends as [Mr.](people/person_798.qmd) and [Mrs. Keble](people/person_795.qmd), [Miss Dyson](people/person_464.qmd), and [Dr. Moberly](people/person_1015.qmd) (later Bishop of Salisbury).  So that external influence had much to do with the developments.  

It has always had the best sale of all my books, yet when I read both it and the [*Pillars of the House*](cmy_books/cmybook_109.qmd) over, for the sake of taking up the broken threads, as well as to see them with older eyes, I found myself preferring the latter, as brighter, and on the whole less pedantic than is the effect of Ethel in parts, and with more of hope throughout.

I think I must mention that [Guizot](people/person_597.qmd)'s public recommendation of the *Heir of Redclyffe* led to the only thoroughly spiteful [review](other_books/otherbook_718.qmd) that ever befell me, in *Household  Words*, written, I imagine, by some blindly jealous admirer of Dickens.

[*Heartsease*](cmy_books/cmybook_19.qmd) was the last book [Lord Raglan](people/person_1276.qmd) read, I was told by [Admiral Sir Stewart](people/person_1277.qmd) who lent it to him.  And [Mr. Butterfield](people/person_247.qmd)was said to be in search of Ethel for a wife.  But [Mrs. T. Mozley](people/person_1062.qmd) had set the fashion of reading books on child life.  By the bye, I wish you would write a notice of the [*Fairy Bower*](other_books/otherbook_240.qmd) and [*Lost Brooch*](other_books/otherbook_78.qmd), also of [*Louisa*](other_books/otherbook_719.qmd), with their wonderful cleverness and irony.

Grace and Mary Anne always remind me of [Dr. Newman](people/person_1084.qmd)'s controversy with [Kingsley](people/person_816.qmd)about truth, the same which resulted in the [*Apologia*](other_books/otherbook_444.qmd).

I have inflicted a long letter on you, but when I once began I could not help going on.

Yours sincerely
C. M. Yonge

---

**Note:** There is a biographical account of Mary Elizabeth Christie (1847-1906) in her *A Tardiness in Nature and Other Papers*  (Manchester: Manchester University Press 1907).
